question: Can a dissipative physical network whose many internal parameters obey fixed local material dynamics be trained for supervised tasks by controlling only its boundary nodes, without directly writing every parameter or contrasting two complete physical states?

key_findings.claim: BEASTAL converts an inaccessible Adaline-like edge update into the closest realizable set of boundary pressures through the pseudoinverse of the network incidence matrix.
key_findings.evidence: For a fully connected single-layer fluidic resistor network, the conductance gradient for mean-squared error is proportional, up to a slowly changing conductance factor, to (y_i-x_j)(target_i-y_i). The desired pressure drop has one component per edge, but the supervisor has only input and output node controls. Multiplying the desired edge-drop vector by the incidence-matrix pseudoinverse projects it into accessible boundary values, after which the material's local pressure-dependent resistance rule performs the update.

key_findings.claim: The projected boundary update is correlated with, but is not equal to, stochastic gradient descent on the internal conductances.
key_findings.evidence: In a 4-input, 6-output regression example, BEASTAL ends at different resistances from exact batch-size-one GD while reaching a solution on the same zero-loss manifold. The update-direction cosine similarity is positive and approaches roughly 0.5 in the 24-dimensional conductance space. Across task sizes, the cubic local rule is not consistently more aligned with GD than the linear rule, so improved performance is not explained by a more exact gradient direction.

key_findings.claim: The linear local rule solves small linear regressions but degrades as both input and output counts grow, whereas a cubic pressure-drop rule produces substantially lower final loss in the reported simulations.
key_findings.evidence: Figure 1 shows arbitrarily low normalized MSE for one-input or one-output examples. The size sweep averages eight random task matrices and the last 400 steps: the linear rule plateaus on multi-input, multi-output tasks, while the cubic rule performs qualitatively better. The cubic experiment also normalizes the projected pressure vector and exponentially anneals the learning rate because raw cubic updates would vanish rapidly, so the gain is due to a combined nonlinear-rule-and-controller recipe.

key_findings.claim: The claimed Iris generalization result is transductive and label-leaking under the paper's own appendix protocol, not a clean held-out test.
key_findings.evidence: The main text says 30 Iris samples train the model and 120 are reserved for testing, with mean test accuracy above 93 percent after a few epochs. Appendix H reveals that at the start of every epoch the target vector for each species is recomputed by passing all 150 samples through the current network and averaging outputs grouped by species. This uses the nominal test inputs and their species labels to construct training targets, invalidating a standard held-out-generalization interpretation even though the subsequent parameter updates use the 30 training samples.

key_findings.claim: Five simulated local material rules learn the transductive Iris task, but the experiment does not demonstrate any physical device or measure training energy.
key_findings.evidence: The Figure 3 inset compares linear and cubic pressure-drop updates, flow- and power-based updates, and an instantaneous pressure-dependent resistance; all average above 85 percent within 2,000 simulated steps over eight runs. The manuscript models steady-state fluidic networks numerically and lists possible electrical, spring, and clogging-channel realizations only in the conclusion. No hardware, noise, finite relaxation, actuator cost, or joule measurement is reported.

key_findings.claim: The method's demonstrated computational class is linear, and adding a hidden layer worsens multi-input, multi-output performance rather than creating a useful nonlinear network.
key_findings.evidence: The studied topology is a single bipartite layer with outputs grounded; positive resistances constrain output ranges, although constant rescaling can compensate. The conclusion reserves nonlinear networks for future work. Appendix A finds hidden layers competitive only when there is a single input or output; for larger tasks the single-layer network with the nonlinear adaptation rule performs best. Nonlinearity in parameter evolution does not make the steady-state input-output computation nonlinear.

key_findings.claim: Boundary-only access reduces direct internal read/write requirements but does not eliminate centralized computation or global supervision.
key_findings.evidence: Each step measures outputs, computes desired outputs and losses, multiplies an edge-sized desired-update vector by a topology-dependent pseudoinverse, imposes every boundary value, waits for steady-state minimization, and switches material modality. The nonlinear version additionally computes a global vector norm and time-dependent annealing schedule. These operations are materially different from reading or programming every resistance, but they are external controller responsibilities.

method.core_idea: Project the internal Adaline conductance update desired for a supervised example onto the pressure differences that can be induced solely through accessible boundary nodes, then let fixed local material physics update every internal edge in parallel.
method.mechanism: A measurement phase clamps inputs, allows a power-minimizing network to settle, and reads outputs. An external controller forms per-edge gradient-like signals from input-output pressure differences and output error, applies the incidence-matrix pseudoinverse to obtain realizable update-phase boundary pressures, and clamps those boundaries. Each resistance then evolves according to its own local pressure, flow, power, or instantaneous constitutive rule. For cubic updates, the controller normalizes the projected vector and exponentially anneals a global learning rate.
assumptions: The physical system has a deterministic steady state obtained by minimizing dissipated power or an analogous energy.
Internal resistances change slowly enough that conductance and resistance derivatives can be treated as proportional with a sign change and slowly varying scale.
The topology and incidence matrix are known and its pseudoinverse can be stored or applied by an external controller.
Measurement and update modalities can be switched cleanly, with negligible unintended parameter drift during measurement.
All required boundary pressures can be imposed with adequate range and precision.
The single-layer positive-resistance input-output map is sufficient for the target task, possibly after output rescaling.
Projected edge updates retain enough descent correlation despite the boundary-control space being much smaller than the internal parameter space.
For nonlinear local rules, global normalization and a time-based annealing schedule are available.
Steady-state, noiseless numerical behavior transfers to a realizable material whose evolution rule remains stable and reversible over many updates.

techniques.role: Maps an edge-wise MSE descent target into boundary controls without directly addressing each resistance.
Finds the least-squares realizable node pressures for an overdetermined desired pressure-drop vector.
Separates inference at fixed parameters from a clamped physical adaptation phase.
Lets internal edges update in parallel from only the physical quantity available at each edge.
Emphasizes edges with large projected pressure drops and suppresses mutually cancelling small updates.
Prevents cubic updates from vanishing early and then reduces the controller step to settle near a minimum.
Measures how closely the physically realizable update direction follows exact conductance-space SGD.

evaluations.setting: One-input or one-output linear regression in simulated fully connected fluidic resistor networks
evaluations.metric: Normalized per-sample mean-squared error over training steps
evaluations.result: The linear pressure-drop evolution rule reaches arbitrarily low reported loss on the illustrated small tasks

evaluations.setting: Grid of 1-10 input and 1-10 output linear tasks with eight random matrices per cell
evaluations.metric: Mean normalized MSE over the final 400 steps
evaluations.result: The linear rule degrades on larger two-sided tasks, while the normalized and annealed cubic rule maintains much lower loss across the grid
evaluations.baseline: Linear local resistance rule under the same topology

evaluations.result: The appendix reports 1.2 for a one-shot pseudoinverse realization, 5e-2 for iterative BEASTAL with a linear rule, and 1e-6 for the nonlinear rule
evaluations.baseline: Non-iterative controller given the full task matrix and an optimal but generally unrealizable internal solution

evaluations.metric: Final resistance correspondence and cosine similarity between BEASTAL and exact SGD updates
evaluations.result: The methods reach different internal solutions; BEASTAL's update stays positively aligned and approaches cosine similarity 0.5 in the shown run
evaluations.baseline: Direct batch-size-one gradient descent on every conductance

evaluations.setting: Iris classification with 30 update samples, 120 nominal test samples, five local rules, and eight runs
evaluations.metric: Nominal test accuracy over fewer than 2,000 steps
evaluations.result: Mean accuracy exceeds 93 percent for the main rule after a few epochs and exceeds 85 percent for all five rules, but targets are recomputed using all 150 labeled samples each epoch
evaluations.baseline: Untrained network trajectory; no leakage-free linear classifier is reported

evaluations.setting: Single-layer versus one-hidden-layer simulated networks on representative multi-input, multi-output tasks
evaluations.metric: Absolute final loss with variability over the final 100 steps
evaluations.result: Hidden networks work for one-sided tasks but underperform the single-layer cubic-rule network when both input and output counts exceed one
evaluations.baseline: Single fully connected layer with linear or cubic local rule

limitations: Author-stated: the present computation remains linear; nonlinear networks and more expressive tasks are left for future work.
Author-stated: positive resistances constrain the unscaled linear task matrix, and hidden layers degrade performance on general multi-input, multi-output tasks.

Reviewer-identified: all central results are in silico steady-state simulations; no proposed material is built and no training time, actuator energy, dissipated energy, drift, noise, or endurance is measured.

Reviewer-identified: the Iris target-token procedure uses all 150 samples grouped by true species every epoch, leaking nominal test inputs and labels into training and invalidating a conventional held-out accuracy claim.

Reviewer-identified: boundary-only control still requires centralized loss computation, knowledge of topology, an incidence pseudoinverse, an edge-sized intermediate vector, synchronized modality switching, and precise boundary clamps.

Reviewer-identified: the best nonlinear result adds global vector normalization and a hand-set exponential schedule, so performance cannot be attributed solely to an intuitive autonomous local material law.
Reviewer-identified: comparison with exact GD focuses on direction correlation and endpoint differences, not matched convergence rate, sample efficiency, energy, controller complexity, or robustness.
Reviewer-identified: regression matrices are sampled under a row-sum constraint and no out-of-distribution, nonlinear, high-dimensional, or real sensing task is evaluated.

Reviewer-identified: eight runs and mostly heatmaps or trajectories provide limited uncertainty analysis; several strong claims such as broad robustness are not backed by systematic perturbation sweeps.
Reviewer-identified: the claim of avoiding large-scale memory is not quantified against two-state coupled learning, and applying a dense pseudoinverse may itself scale poorly with topology changes.
failure_modes: Rank deficiency of the incidence map can project away edge-update components essential for lowering loss as tasks scale.
Nonlinear local rules can stall when local driving vanishes or become unstable when boundary forcing is too large, necessitating global normalization and annealing.
Resistances may become negative, saturate, drift, or hit physical bounds not represented in the idealized simulations.
Finite relaxation or updates during measurement can break the assumed separation between inference and learning modalities.
Sensor and actuator noise can corrupt the small difference between measured and desired outputs used to generate boundary drives.
Topology damage or rewiring invalidates a precomputed pseudoinverse unless the controller re-identifies the network.
Hidden or nonlinear architectures may have multiple equilibria and need control signals not captured by the linear derivation.
A transductive class-prototype protocol can overstate generalization if nominal test labels influence targets.
Controller and clamping energy may dominate any savings from parallel internal adaptation.
reusable_insights: When internal parameters are inaccessible, project a desired parameter-space update into the physically controllable boundary subspace and measure how much descent survives the projection.
Separate claims of spatial locality, autonomy, and absence of centralized computation; a local material update can coexist with a global boundary controller.
Compare physical learning schemes on a full accounting of states, measurements, stored topology, controller arithmetic, settling time, and actuator energy.
Nonlinear adaptation can act as implicit coordinate selection by concentrating change on locally high-error elements even when it is not more gradient-aligned.
Validate projected learning against exact gradients with both angular alignment and actual one-step loss decrease, not cosine alone.
Treat any target construction that uses held-out examples or labels as transductive and report a separate untouched test split.

A credible physical-learning ladder should progress from ideal steady-state simulation to component models, noisy dynamic simulation, a small hardware loop, and end-to-end energy and wall-clock comparison.
open_questions: Can BEASTAL be implemented in a material with bounded positive parameters and distinct, reliable measurement and update timescales?
What fraction of the true gradient survives the incidence projection as graph size, sparsity, depth, and task rank grow?
Can a sparse or local boundary controller replace the dense pseudoinverse while retaining convergence guarantees?
Does the cubic-rule advantage persist under matched normalization and annealing controls for the linear rule?
How does the method compare with coupled learning and equilibrium propagation under matched hardware, precision, settling, and energy budgets?
Can a leakage-free Iris split or a larger untouched benchmark reproduce the classification result?
What nonlinear physical architectures admit an analogous boundary projection without unstable multiple equilibria?
Can topology changes be detected and the controller adapted without reading all internal elements?
Is there a convergence bound in terms of the controllability projection, material response law, and condition number of the incidence map?

competitive_landscape.title: Supervised learning in physical networks: From machine learning to learning machines
competitive_landscape.difference: Stern et al. derive coupled learning rules for equilibrium and steady-state flow or elastic networks, using free and clamped physical states to approximate a supervised gradient through local contrasts. BEASTAL avoids storing or comparing every edge's two-state response and accepts a pre-existing intuitive material rule, but moves more work into a topology-aware boundary projection and presently handles only linear maps.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv record for the Phys. Rev. X 2021 article

competitive_landscape.title: Demonstration of Decentralized, Physics-Driven Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Dillavou et al. physically demonstrate coupled learning in self-adjusting variable-resistor networks, including local comparison circuitry and real nonidealities. The reviewed paper's boundary-only projection may simplify internal instrumentation and allow native material laws, but remains a simulation and does not yet establish that its measurement/update modes or nonlinear rule can be built efficiently.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv abstract record current when checked

competitive_landscape.title: A fast algorithm to simulate nonlinear resistive networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Scellier develops an exact coordinate-descent simulator for nonlinear resistive networks and demonstrates dramatic simulation scaling gains for equilibrium-propagation-style training. That work addresses nonlinear inference architectures and evaluation throughput, whereas BEASTAL contributes a boundary-control learning rule; using the faster simulator would expose whether BEASTAL's present 10-by-10 scale and hidden-layer failure are fundamental or tooling-limited.

competitive_landscape.title: Experimental Demonstration of Coupled Learning in Elastic Networks
competitive_landscape.difference: Altman et al. show an elastic network learning a simple symmetry task through iterative tuning of spring rest lengths under coupled states. It supplies physical evidence that local adaptive materials can learn across modalities, while BEASTAL broadens the simulated supervised task class and native-rule concept but has not demonstrated a spring or fluidic device.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv abstract record current when checked

competitive_landscape.title: How to Train Your Resistive Network: Generalized Equilibrium Propagation and Analytical Learning
competitive_landscape.difference: Lin et al. derive exact graph-theoretic gradients for resistive networks, require readout only at the output layer, and show that updating a subset of resistors need not strongly degrade performance. Their approach directly programs selected parameters and emphasizes gradient exactness; BEASTAL instead tolerates an approximate projected direction and delegates updates to native local physics, trading exactness and expressivity for less internal access.
competitive_landscape.source_version: arXiv abstract record current when checked

novelty_assessment.author_claim: The authors claim the closest Adaline analogue for boundary-accessible dissipative systems, enabling supervised regression and classification with intuitive native local evolution rules rather than engineered contrastive edge rules or direct internal parameter access.
novelty_assessment.evidence: The incidence-pseudoinverse controller turns desired edge-wise descent signals into boundary values, and simulated linear networks learn under several pressure-, flow-, power-, or constitutive-response rules; nonlinear adaptation yields the strongest regression results.
novelty_assessment.reviewer_inference: The distinctive contribution is the boundary projection that makes an arbitrary native edge law participate in approximate supervised descent without a twin network. It does not establish autonomous or computation-free learning: the external controller still computes loss, an edge-sized signal, a pseudoinverse transform, global normalization, and annealing. Coupled learning already supplies local physical supervision with hardware evidence, while later analytical work offers output-only exact gradients. BEASTAL is best viewed as a promising controller-material interface for simple linear networks whose hardware and scaling advantages remain unverified.
